blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The mode is the value or category that occurs most often in a dataset.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Sometimes the question is neither “where does the data balance?” (mean) nor “what is in the middle?” (median) but “what shows up most often?”. That is the mode. It is the only one of the three that works for nominal data: you cannot average or rank blood groups, but you can count which one is commonest.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Blood groups recorded for 20 patients: O 9, A 6, B 4, AB 1. Mode = O. Mean and median are undefined, because blood group has no numeric value and no order.

A dataset can be unimodal (one peak), bimodal (two peaks) or multimodal (more than two).

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
For grouped data, the modal class is the class with the highest frequency f₁. Let f₀ and f₂ be the frequencies of the classes just below and just above it. The peak should lean toward the heavier neighbour. Draw a line from the top-left corner of the modal bar to the top-left corner of the next bar, and another from the top-right corner of the modal bar to the top-right corner of the previous bar (the grey lines in the figure below). By similar triangles, they cross at a distance d from L where d ÷ (h − d) = (f₁ − f₀) ÷ (f₁ − f₂). Solving for d gives

Mode = L + [(f₁ − f₀) ÷ (2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)] × h

blocks.label: Worked Calculation: grouped mode
blocks.html:
1. Modal class: 10 to <12 (f₁ = 12). L = 10, h = 2, f₀ = 5 (class below), f₂ = 9 (class above).
  2. Mode = 10 + [(12 − 5) ÷ (24 − 5 − 9)] × 2 = 10 + (7 ÷ 10) × 2 = 11.4 kg.

The peak leans right of the class mid-point (11) because the class above (9 children) is heavier than the class below (5 children).

blocks.alt: Histogram of today’s 30 children with grouped mean, median and mode
blocks.caption: Figure 2.1. Histogram of today’s 30 children. The grey lines are the construction behind the grouped-mode formula; they cross at the grouped mode, 11.40 kg. The grouped median (11.67 kg) and grouped mean (11.80 kg) lie to its right.

points.html: The mode is the only measure of central tendency valid for nominal data.
Grouped data: Mode = L + [(f₁ − f₀) ÷ (2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)] × h. It needs equal class widths around the modal class.

Empirical relation. A classical rule of thumb for moderately skewed, single-peaked distributions: mode ≈ 3 × median − 2 × mean, equivalently mean − mode ≈ 3(mean − median). It is an approximation, not an identity; §3.9 checks it on a smooth skewed curve (Figure 3.1). For today’s 30 children: 3 × 11.67 − 2 × 11.8 = 35.0 − 23.6 = 11.4 kg, which matches the grouped mode. Use it when the mode is hard to estimate, and do not trust it for strongly skewed or multimodal data.
Bimodality in health data can signal two subgroups mixed together, for example two disease subtypes with different typical ages of onset.
In small samples the mode is the least stable of the three measures: a single changed value can shift which value is commonest.
